notes.title: Project Alpha — Architecture Document
notes.content:
Project Alpha — Real-Time Collaboration Architecture

Overview:
Project Alpha enables real-time collaborative editing for TechFlow AI documents. Multiple users can simultaneously edit, see each other's cursors, and receive instant updates.

Architecture:
- CRDT-based conflict resolution (Yjs library)
- WebSocket connections for real-time sync
- Document state stored in PostgreSQL (serialized CRDT state)
- Redis pub/sub for multi-server coordination
- Awareness protocol for cursor positions and user presence

Key Design Decisions:
1. CRDT over OT (Operational Transform): CRDTs are simpler to reason about, work offline, and don't require a central server for conflict resolution.
2. Yjs: Best-in-class CRDT library. Active community, good TypeScript support, extensible.
3. WebSocket over SSE: Need bidirectional communication for both sync and awareness.
4. PostgreSQL for persistence: Already our primary DB. CRDT state is just a binary blob column.

Performance Targets:
- Latency: <100ms for edit propagation between users
- Concurrent users per doc: Up to 20 (v1)
- Document size: Up to 500KB (before pagination)
- Offline support: Full offline editing with sync on reconnect

Status: V1 shipped January 2026. Performance meets targets. Next: V2 with comments and suggestions.

notes.title: Database Migration Plan — Q1 2026
notes.content:
Database Migration Plan

Objective: Migrate from single PostgreSQL instance to read replicas + connection pooling.

Current State:
- Single RDS PostgreSQL 14 instance (db.r6g.xlarge)
- 120GB data, ~500 connections peak
- P95 query latency: 45ms (acceptable but growing)
- CPU utilization: 65% average, 85% peaks

Target State:
- Primary + 2 read replicas
- PgBouncer for connection pooling
- P95 query latency: <20ms
- CPU utilization: <40% average

Migration Steps:
1. [DONE] Add PgBouncer in front of primary (connection pooling)
2. [DONE] Identify read-heavy queries for replica routing
3. [IN PROGRESS] Set up read replicas (Priya handling infrastructure)
4. [PENDING] Update application code to route reads to replicas
5. [PENDING] Load test with replica routing
6. [PENDING] Monitor for replication lag issues

Risks:
- Replication lag for real-time features (mitigation: sticky sessions for collaboration)
- Connection pool exhaustion during peaks (mitigation: queue + retry)
- Schema migrations become more complex (mitigation: use pg_logical_replication)

Timeline: Complete by end of March 2026
Owner: Mike Torres (code), Priya Sharma (infra)
Reviewer: Alex Chen

notes.title: Code Review Guidelines
notes.content:
TechFlow Engineering — Code Review Guidelines

Purpose:
Code review exists to improve code quality, share knowledge, and catch bugs. It is NOT a gatekeeping exercise or a power dynamic.

Expectations:
- Author: PR description explains WHY not just WHAT. Include testing notes.
- Reviewer: Review within 4 business hours. Be constructive, not harsh.
- Size: Aim for <400 lines changed. Break large changes into stacked PRs.

What to Look For:
1. Correctness: Does the code do what it claims?
2. Design: Is the approach reasonable? Could it be simpler?
3. Performance: Any obvious N+1 queries, memory leaks, or inefficiencies?
4. Security: Input validation, auth checks, data exposure risks?
5. Tests: Are critical paths tested? Are edge cases considered?
6. Readability: Can another engineer understand this in 6 months?

Comment Conventions:
- 'nit:' — minor style preference, non-blocking
- 'suggestion:' — alternative approach, non-blocking
- 'question:' — I don't understand, please explain
- 'blocker:' — must fix before merge

Approval Policy:
- 1 approval required for most PRs
- 2 approvals for: database migrations, auth changes, infra changes
- Alex auto-approves for emergency hotfixes (with post-mortem review)

SLA:
- Initial review: Within 4 hours during business hours
- Follow-up review: Within 2 hours
- If blocked >8 hours: Escalate to Alex

notes.title: Performance Benchmarks — API Optimization
notes.content:
API Performance Benchmarks — Post-Optimization

Date: February 12, 2026
Environment: Production (US-West-2)
Tool: k6 load testing + Datadog APM

Endpoint: GET /api/documents (list)
Before optimization:
- P50: 120ms
- P95: 340ms
- P99: 890ms
- Throughput: 200 req/s

After optimization (N+1 fix + query caching):
- P50: 45ms (62% improvement)
- P95: 95ms (72% improvement)
- P99: 210ms (76% improvement)
- Throughput: 580 req/s (190% improvement)

Endpoint: POST /api/documents (create)
- P50: 85ms → 60ms (29% improvement)
- P95: 180ms → 110ms (39% improvement)

Endpoint: GET /api/search
- P50: 200ms → 150ms (25% improvement)
- P95: 500ms → 280ms (44% improvement)
- Note: Search will improve further with Elasticsearch (currently PostgreSQL full-text)

Key Changes Made:
1. Added DataLoader pattern to resolve N+1 queries
2. Implemented Redis caching for document metadata (5-min TTL)
3. Optimized PostgreSQL indexes (added composite index on user_id + updated_at)
4. Reduced payload size with field selection (GraphQL-style ?fields= param)

Next Steps:
- Monitor production metrics for 2 weeks
- Target: Maintain P95 <100ms as user base grows
- Elasticsearch migration will be the next major perf win (Tom's project)

notes.title: Architecture Decision Record — Real-Time Sync
notes.content:
ADR-003: Real-Time Synchronization Strategy

Status: Accepted
Date: January 5, 2026
Deciders: Mike Torres, Alex Chen

Context:
TechFlow needs real-time collaborative editing. Multiple users must be able to edit the same document simultaneously without conflicts.

Decision:
Use CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type) via the Yjs library for real-time document synchronization.

Alternatives Considered:
1. Operational Transform (OT) — Used by Google Docs
   - Pro: Battle-tested at scale
   - Con: Requires central server, complex implementation, poor offline support

2. Last-Write-Wins (LWW)
   - Pro: Simple
   - Con: Data loss when concurrent edits occur

3. CRDT via Yjs (CHOSEN)
   - Pro: Offline support, no central server needed, mathematically proven conflict-free
   - Con: Larger document state, less control over merge behavior

Consequences:
- We get offline editing for free
- Document state is a binary blob (harder to query directly)
- Need WebSocket infrastructure for sync (Priya to set up)
- Undo/redo requires CRDT-aware implementation

Validation:
- Prototype tested with 10 concurrent users — smooth
- Performance acceptable up to 500KB document size
- Network usage: ~2KB per keystroke (acceptable)

Review Date: April 2026 (after 3 months in production)

notes.title: Incident Postmortem — Feb 15 Downtime
notes.content:
Incident Postmortem — February 15, 2026

Severity: P2 (partial service degradation)
Duration: 23 minutes (1:42 PM - 2:05 PM Pacific)
Impact: Document saves failing for ~30% of users

Timeline:
- 1:42 PM: Monitoring alert fires (error rate spike)
- 1:44 PM: Mike investigates, sees PostgreSQL connection pool exhaustion
- 1:48 PM: Identified cause: A runaway query from a new feature flag was holding connections
- 1:52 PM: Disabled feature flag via admin panel
- 1:55 PM: Connection pool draining, some requests recovering
- 2:05 PM: Full recovery confirmed. Error rate back to baseline.

Root Cause:
A new feature (document auto-save frequency increase) was enabled via feature flag without load testing. The increased save frequency (every 5s instead of 30s) multiplied DB connections by 6x, exhausting the PgBouncer pool.

Contributing Factors:
- Feature flag enabled without gradual rollout (jumped to 100%)
- No connection pool monitoring alert at 80% threshold
- Auto-save frequency change wasn't flagged as high-risk

Action Items:
1. [Priya] Add alert at 80% connection pool utilization — DONE
2. [Mike] Add load testing step to feature flag rollout checklist
3. [Alex] Require gradual rollout (10% → 50% → 100%) for DB-heavy features
4. [Tom] Add connection pool dashboard to Datadog

Lessons Learned:
- Feature flags are powerful but need discipline
- Any change that multiplies DB load needs load testing
- Quick recovery thanks to good monitoring and clear runbook

notes.title: Engineering Onboarding Document
notes.content:
TechFlow Engineering — Onboarding Guide
(Maintained by Mike Torres)

Welcome to the TechFlow engineering team! This doc helps you get productive quickly.

1. Local Development Setup:
- Clone repo: git clone git@github.com:techflow-ai/techflow.git
- Install dependencies: pnpm install
- Set up environment: cp .env.example .env.local (ask Mike for secrets)
- Run database: docker compose up db redis
- Run migrations: pnpm db:migrate
- Start dev server: pnpm dev (runs on localhost:3000)

2. Architecture Overview:
- Frontend: Next.js 14 (App Router), React 19, TailwindCSS
- Backend: Next.js API routes + standalone Express server for WebSockets
- Database: PostgreSQL 14 (RDS) + Redis (ElastiCache)
- Search: Elasticsearch (OpenSearch Service)
- Infrastructure: AWS (ECS Fargate), managed by Priya
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions → AWS ECR → ECS deployment

3. Key Repos:
- techflow (main monorepo — everything lives here)
- techflow-infra (Terraform, Priya's domain)
- techflow-docs (public documentation site)

4. Development Workflow:
- Branch from main: feature/TICKET-description
- Write code + tests
- Open PR, request review (1 approval needed, 2 for DB/auth/infra changes)
- Merge to main (squash merge)
- Auto-deploys to staging
- Manual promote to production (Alex or Mike approve)

5. Key Contacts:
- Architecture questions: Mike Torres or Alex Chen
- Frontend: Lisa Nakamura
- Search: Tom Bradford
- Infrastructure/DevOps: Priya Sharma
- Product/design: Tina Rodriguez + Derek Lam

6. Useful Links:

- API docs: localhost:3000/api-docs (Swagger)
- Datadog: app.datadoghq.com (credentials in 1Password)
- GitHub: github.com/techflow-ai

notes.title: Integration Testing Best Practices
notes.content:
Integration Testing Best Practices — TechFlow
(Written by Mike Torres, Sprint 22 action item)

1. Database Setup:
- Use a dedicated test database (not dev)
- Reset database state between test suites (not between individual tests — too slow)
- Seed with minimal fixtures (not full production-like data)
- Use transactions for test isolation: Begin transaction → run test → rollback

2. API Tests:
- Use supertest for HTTP endpoint testing
- Always test: Happy path, error cases, auth (unauthorized, forbidden), validation
- Mock external services (Elasticsearch, email, etc.) — don't call real services in CI
- Assert on response body AND status code

3. Avoiding Flaky Tests:
- Never rely on timing (no setTimeout in tests)
- Use database transactions for isolation (see #1)
- Mock Date.now() when testing time-dependent logic
- Use deterministic IDs in test fixtures
- If testing async operations: Use proper await, not arbitrary delays

4. Performance:
- Test suite should complete in <5 minutes (CI budget)
- Parallelize where possible (Jest workers)
- Skip heavy tests locally with .skip() — they run in CI
- Use --bail flag in CI to fail fast

5. What to Integration Test:
- API endpoints (most critical)
- Database queries (especially complex joins/aggregations)
- Authentication/authorization flows
- Webhook processing
- Background job execution

6. What NOT to Integration Test:
- UI components (use unit tests + Storybook)
- External service behavior (use contract tests or mocks)
- Performance (use dedicated load tests, not CI)
